name: Stomach vacuum / waist training

card.summary: Pulling the belly in to train the deep abdominal muscle for a smaller-looking waist; little research exists on it for appearance.
card.note: Sources on abdominal exercise say it does not by itself reduce abdominal fat.

quick.overview:
The stomach vacuum is an exercise in which the abdomen is drawn inward, aimed at the transversus abdominis, the deepest abdominal muscle. Forum users discuss it as a way to get a tighter-looking waist.

Sources are thin. A looksmax.org thread has a user asking whether others lost the ability to do it and reporting it came back with renewed training.
quick.mechanism: The transversus abdominis is one of four abdominal wall muscles. Wikipedia notes that whether training this deep core muscle specifically is worthwhile is disputed, and that abdominal exercise alone is not enough to reduce abdominal fat or girth according to a 2011 study.
quick.risks: No harms data were found for the exercise. Community talk of 'waist training' sometimes also refers to compression garments, which this entry does not cover.

lead: The stomach vacuum is an abdominal exercise in which the belly button is drawn inward toward the spine by contracting the deep abdominal muscles, mainly the transversus abdominis, with little use of the diaphragm.[3] People practice it for a flatter, tighter-looking midsection and a smaller apparent waist; Wikipedia says it is used for a leaner midsection in bodybuilding competitions.[3]

The transversus abdominis is the deepest of the flat abdominal muscles and is often called the corset muscle because pulling the abdomen inward creates girdle-like tension around the midsection.[4] Looksmaxxing discussion treats training it as a way to improve waist appearance without compression garments.

Community material is limited to short forum posts, such as a looksmax.org thread in which a user says he nearly lost the ability to perform it two years earlier and can do it easily again after resuming training.[2] No clinical studies were found.

paras: Wikipedia describes the vacuum exercise as contracting the internal abdominal muscles, with repetitions that can serve as light aerobic or light strength work.[3] Strength can be built, it says, by drawing the muscle in further, contracting harder or holding longer, and some people use a string tied at navel level as feedback.[3] Wikipedia also notes disputed benefit and healthiness of doing it while lifting.[3]

The abdominal exercise article describes the transversus abdominis as part of the four-muscle abdominal wall and says focused training of this deep core muscle is disputed, with some experts recommending broader regimens.[1]

Wikipedia describes progressions in general terms: widening the range of motion, holding longer, working against gravity, or using rapid flutters or interval-style sets.[3] The string method gives feedback by tying a string at navel level at roughly three-quarters of maximum vacuum, so that the string tightens when the belly relaxes and expands.[3] Wikipedia also lists claimed benefits including a flatter-looking abdomen in bodybuilding competitions, core stability, belly-dance flutters and a belief that the pressure aids digestion, while flagging weak sourcing for several of these statements.[3]

BarBend traces the vacuum to yoga, where drawing the abdomen in appears as abdominal drawing in the Uddiyana Bandha posture, and reports historian Conor Heffernan's account that it entered bodybuilding in the early 1900s, when displays of muscle control were popular, with Maxick as the first physique celebrity to use it [11]. Frank Zane, a three-time Mr. Olympia winner, is the figure most associated with it in professional bodybuilding; his 1979 Mr. Olympia pose, photographed by his wife Christine, became iconic partly for his abdominal control [11].

Terrick El Guindy, speaking in a FitnessVolt report, traces the modern vacuum pose to Zane and Arnold Schwarzenegger, says it faded for years and then returned as a response to distended midsections, called bubble guts, in the Phil Heath era, and credits Chris Bumstead as one of the first Classic Physique competitors to show it to judges even when it was not required [12]. Heffernan links the Classic Physique division's interest to the 1990s, when a distended abdomen sometimes attributed to growth hormone misuse was common [11].

BarBend states that the vacuum is a required pose in the Classic Physique division and can make the waist look tighter [11]. Chris Cormier, quoted in the same FitnessVolt piece, argues that vacuums became a big topic after YouTubers and bloggers emphasized them, that anyone can learn the pose with practice but not everyone looks good doing it, and that a distended stomach is a matter of how someone trains and eats [12].

Outside bodybuilding, abdominal drawing-in is used in physical therapy. BarBend reports that it is used to recover neuromuscular control in athletes with damaged trunk-stability muscles and is sometimes prescribed for chronic low back pain, citing studies of deep abdominal exercise and transversus abdominis thickness (Lee and colleagues, 2015), core stabilization with abdominal drawing-in in sedentary workers with chronic low back pain (Saiklang and colleagues, 2022) and a review of transversus abdominis development in preventing and treating low back pain (Lynders, 2019) [11]. BarBend also states that the exercise does not directly cause fat loss and describes the narrower look as an optical effect, though some bodybuilders believe regular practice helps a midsection look tighter once body fat is low enough [11].

The phrase waist training is also used for wearing compression garments such as corsets; this entry concerns the muscle exercise. Related practices include hypopressive exercises, which Wikipedia says are thought to raise abdominal wall and pelvic floor tone and reduce resting waist circumference.[3]

Hypopressive exercises also engage the transversus abdominis, through reflex contraction of the abdominal wall rather than voluntary effort, and are thought to raise the baseline tone of the abdominal wall and pelvic floor, which may reduce resting waist circumference.[3] Corset-style waist training is a separate practice with its own history and is not covered here.

sections.h: Use in bodybuilding and lifting communities
paras: Wikipedia describes the vacuum as used for a flatter-looking abdomen in bodybuilding competition poses.[3] T Nation training logs show members listing stomach vacuums as part of daily routines, for example as 2 sets of 15 plus one of 30 in a morning bodyweight circuit, as one set of 20 before pressing work, and as 1 to 2 sets between abdominal work sets.[5][6][7] A contest-prep log mentions a 'vacuum' pose alongside body-weight and waist measurements, and another member advises holding the stomach in during a side-triceps pose.[8][9] In another thread a member who has no visible abs says he can still do a stomach vacuum, and notes that oblique development widens the waist.[10]

The abdominal exercise article states that whether abdominal exercise reduces belly fat is highly disputed, citing a 2011 study that found abdominal exercises alone were not enough to reduce abdominal fat and girth, and adds that fat reduction requires an energy deficit.[1] Wikipedia notes that the effectiveness of transversus abdominis training is debated, with some reviews finding its function does not reliably predict low back pain outcomes.[4]

Wikipedia's own caveats note that the vacuum page's sources for several claims are weak or marked as needing citations, which matches the absence of published trials on the exercise itself.[3] The visual effect people seek, a narrower-looking waist, depends on both the muscles of the abdominal wall and on abdominal fat, which the abdominal exercise article says exercise alone does not reduce without an energy deficit.[1]

No studies found of the stomach vacuum for waist size or appearance. Related studies of abdominal drawing-in as a rehabilitation exercise for low back pain are summarized by fitness media, which cite trials of deep abdominal exercise and core stabilization in people with chronic low back pain [11].

timeline.event: Drawing the abdomen in enters bodybuilding as muscle-control displays are popular, with Maxick named as the first physique celebrity to use it. [11]
Frank Zane's Mr. Olympia pose, showing his abdominal control, becomes an iconic image of the vacuum. [11]
Distended abdomens, sometimes attributed to growth hormone misuse, become common in bodybuilding, later shaping interest in the vacuum. [11][12]
A study reported that abdominal exercise alone is not enough to reduce abdominal fat or girth. [1]

lore.intro: Discussion on looksmax.org is brief and anecdotal [2], while T Nation training logs mention stomach vacuums as a routine warm-up or posing practice.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: The stomach vacuum skill can be lost and regained with training.
claims.believers: One user reports that he could barely do it two years earlier and can do it easily after training again [2].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this.

claims.claim: Stomach vacuums tighten the waist for a smaller-looking midsection
claims.believers: Lifters list vacuums in daily routines and as a posing skill, and describe them as a way to improve midsection control.[5][6][9]
claims.experts: No published studies have measured waist circumference after stomach vacuum training; related hypopressive exercises are thought by some to reduce resting waist circumference.[3]

claims.claim: Vacuum training can be done between lifting sets
claims.believers: Some T Nation members report doing 1 to 2 sets between abdominal work sets.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the benefit and healthiness of combining the vacuum with heavy lifting is disputed.[3]

angle.text: Practitioners use the stomach vacuum to build control of the deep abdominal wall so the waist and stomach look tighter. The change is in muscle tone and posture of the midsection rather than in body fat.
